  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Tasha was twenty-six when the police pulled her over on a Friday night in late October, driving home from a parent-teacher conference that had run long. She remembered the blue lights flashing in her rearview mirror, the way her hands trembled as she reached for her registration in the glove compartment. The officer had smelled of alcohol when he leaned into her window—sour and sharp, a smell she would later come to know as the scent of danger itself. She had done everything right: hands on the wheel, movements slow, voice calm. It had not mattered. What happened next on that empty stretch of road had rewritten something fundamental in how Tasha understood the world. The sound of his voice shouting, the crack of her head against the door frame as he yanked her from the car, the boot against her ribs while she lay on the asphalt—these moments lodged themselves in her body like shrapnel that would never stop moving.

In the months that followed, Tasha found herself shrinking. She had always been the kind of person colleagues and students could count on—warm, steady, present—but something in her had broken its moorings. She began to cancel her afternoon counseling sessions, telling herself she was just tired. And she was tired, bone-tired in a way that sleep could not touch, a fatigue that sat behind her eyes and made the simplest decisions feel impossible. But the fatigue was also a trap: when she was exhausted, her guard dropped, and that was when the memories would rush in, unbidden and vivid, as though she were still lying on that cold asphalt. She came to understand exhaustion as a kind of vulnerability, and yet she could not escape it.

The school where she worked became a landscape of hidden hazards. A student slamming a locker door sent Tasha’s heart into her throat, her field of vision narrowing, her palms wet. She learned to brace herself before walking through the hallways between classes, scanning for sudden movements the way a soldier might scan for tripwires. A colleague touching her shoulder from behind made her flinch so violently that she started sitting with her back to the wall in the staff room. Even when she locked her office door during her lunch break, her shoulders stayed tight, her ears tuned to every footstep in the corridor. She could not relax anywhere. Safety, she had learned, was something she could no longer trust.

Small pleasures became sources of dread. When a student handed her a drawing they had made for her, something hopeful and bright, Tasha felt a stab of fear instead of warmth. She had come to believe that happiness was a trap, that letting herself feel hopeful would only make her more vulnerable to the next blow. She started declining invitations to happy hours and weekend gatherings with friends, telling them she was swamped with work. But the isolation grew into something more painful than she had expected. In the quiet of her apartment, she would scroll through photos of friends laughing together and feel the distance between them as an actual, physical thing—a glass wall she could see through but never touch. She was certain there was something fundamentally wrong with her, some defect that others could sense, and that her marriage was held together by nothing more than her husband’s patience. She replayed the night of the traffic stop again and again, searching for what she might have done differently, and each time she landed on the same verdict: if she had been calmer, or more deferential, or said the right words, it would not have happened. The shame of that belief settled into her bones.

What finally brought Tasha to seek help was a moment at work she could not talk herself out of. A father arrived at the school office smelling of beer, and the smell hit her before she saw him—that same sour, sharp scent—and she excused herself to the bathroom and vomited into the toilet. Her principal found her there, trembling, and asked if she was all right. Tasha said she was fine. But she was not fine. She sat in that bathroom stall for twenty minutes, unable to stand up, certain that if she walked back into the hallway she would fall apart completely. She was afraid of what she might become if she did not find a way to stop the unraveling. She wanted to go back to being the person who could meet a student’s eyes without flinching, the wife who could sit on the couch without scanning the windows. She did not know if that person still existed. But she was desperate enough to find out.
